title: atac_project
text:
Cardiometabolic diseases—including heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes—represent a major global health burden and arise from a combination of environmental and genetic factors. Large-scale genetic studies, such as genome-wide association studies (GWAS), have identified numerous genetic variants associated with increased disease risk. Notably, the majority of these variants are not located within protein-coding regions of the genome, but instead occur in noncoding regulatory DNA. This suggests that many disease-associated variants may influence gene expression rather than directly altering protein structure.
Regulatory DNA elements, such as enhancers and promoters, play a crucial role in controlling gene expression by interacting with transcription factors and other regulatory proteins. The activity of these elements is strongly influenced by chromatin accessibility. Chromatin can exist in either an open (accessible) or closed (inaccessible) state, which determines whether regulatory proteins can bind DNA and activate transcription. As a result, mapping chromatin accessibility provides key insights into which regions of the genome are functionally active in specific cell types.
One powerful method for measuring chromatin accessibility is ATAC-seq, which uses a transposase enzyme to identify regions of open chromatin across the genome. This technique enables high-resolution profiling of regulatory landscapes and has become an essential tool for linking noncoding genetic variation to gene regulatory function.
The liver is a central organ in metabolic regulation, playing critical roles in glucose homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and energy balance. Because of these functions, liver cells are highly relevant to the development of cardiometabolic diseases. Genetic variants that affect regulatory regions in liver tissue may alter chromatin accessibility and disrupt normal gene expression patterns, ultimately contributing to disease risk.
In this project, we investigate chromatin accessibility in liver tissue using ATAC-seq and examine its relationship to genes associated with cardiometabolic disease. By focusing on regulatory regions near these genes, we aim to understand how noncoding genetic variation influences gene expression in a tissue-specific context. This work will provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying cardiometabolic disease and may help identify potential targets for future therapeutic intervention.




Enrichment of cardiometabolic genes in ATAC peaks

Odds ratio ~2.07 (p < 0.001)




 _Findings -This heatmap shows the distribution of ATAC-seq peaks across cardiometabolic genes in different genomic regions (promoter, exon, intron, intergenic). Darker coloring indicates higher chromatin accessibility.
The presence of ATAC peaks across many cardiometabolic genes indicates that these genes are associated with open chromatin, which reflects active regulatory DNA. This supports the hypothesis that regulatory elements play a role in disease risk.
There is strong enrichment of peaks in intronic and promoter regions, while exon regions show very low accessibility. Since promoters and introns commonly contain regulatory elements such as enhancers and transcription start sites, this suggests that gene regulation—rather than coding sequence changes—is a key mechanism influencing these genes.
Intronic regions show the highest level of accessibility across many genes, including FTO, TCF7L2, PPARG, and INSR. This is important because introns often contain enhancer elements that control gene expression in a tissue-specific manner. This supports the idea that regulatory DNA contributes to cardiometabolic risk.
Although the heatmap does not directly compare multiple tissues, the data is derived from liver ATAC-seq. Therefore, the observed chromatin accessibility patterns reflect regulatory activity in liver cells, supporting the liver-specific aspect of the hypothesis.
